practice_questions.text: How does Shelley present the theme of power in 'Ozymandias'? Analyse specific language and structural choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison of how power is presented. Perceptive analysis of language, form and structure with well-integrated context. Precise subject terminology throughout.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful, developed response with clear analysis of methods. Context integrated effectively.
Mid band (16-20): Clear understanding with explained analysis. Some relevant context.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained comments on language with relevant references.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with some relevant references.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Shelley in 'Ozymandias' and one other poet from the anthology present the effects of power. Use specific quotations from both poems.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should compare methods, not just content. Strong answers will:
• Analyse language choices in both poems (e.g. 'sneer of cold command' vs equivalent from chosen poem)
• Compare structural choices (e.g. broken sonnet vs chosen poem's form)
• Discuss how context shapes each poet's message about power
• Use comparative connectives throughout (similarly, whereas, in contrast)
• Integrate subject terminology precisely

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shelley uses the image of the desert to convey his message about power.
practice_questions.marks:
• The desert symbolises the vastness of time and nature (1 mark)
• 'lone and level sands stretch far away' — alliteration of 'l' creates a sweeping, empty tone (1 mark)
• The desert has consumed Ozymandias's 'Works' — irony that nothing remains (1 mark)
• Nature is presented as the ultimate power, indifferent to human achievement (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: What is the effect of the framing narrative in 'Ozymandias'?
practice_questions.marks:
• Creates distance between the reader and Ozymandias (1 mark)
• We hear from a speaker → a traveller → a sculptor → the king — each layer removes us further from his power (1 mark)
• Reinforces how completely his influence has faded (1 mark)
• The indirect telling mirrors the idea that Ozymandias's voice can no longer be heard directly (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explain how Shelley uses irony in 'Ozymandias' to criticise tyranny.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive, detailed analysis. Identifies dramatic irony in the inscription 'Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!' — the boast is now meaningless as nothing remains. Links to Shelley's radical politics and opposition to monarchy.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear, explained analysis with relevant quotations and some context.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some relevant references.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments with limited reference to the text.

practice_questions.text: How does Shelley's disruption of the sonnet form contribute to the meaning of 'Ozymandias'?
practice_questions.marks:
• The irregular rhyme scheme (ABAB ACDC EDE FEF) breaks the traditional sonnet pattern (1 mark)
• This mirrors the destruction of Ozymandias's empire — the form is 'ruined' like the statue (1 mark)
• The enjambment across lines creates a flowing, unstoppable movement — like the passage of time (1 mark)
• The single-stanza structure contrasts with the traditional volta, suggesting there is no resolution — power simply decays (1 mark)

before.exam_tip_html: In the comparison question, don’t just describe what happens in each poem — compare how the poets present their ideas. For Ozymandias, focus on Shelley’s use of irony and the broken sonnet form. A strong response will analyse the effect of specific language choices (e.g. “sneer of cold command”) and link them to Shelley’s radical political beliefs.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Blake in 'London' and Agard in 'Checking Out Me History' present the abuse of power. Use quotations from both poems.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison. Perceptive analysis of methods in both poems. Well-integrated context (Industrial Revolution for Blake; post-colonial identity for Agard). Precise terminology.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful, developed comparison with clear analysis.
Mid band (16-20): Clear, explained comparison with relevant quotations.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comments comparing both poems.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with limited comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present protest in 'London' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Analyse language choices that convey protest (e.g. 'mind-forg'd manacles')
• Compare structural methods (e.g. regular vs irregular form)
• Discuss how context shapes each poet's protest
• Use comparative connectives throughout
• Integrate AO3 context precisely

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Blake uses the metaphor 'mind-forg'd manacles' to present the theme of oppression.
practice_questions.marks:
• 'Manacles' = chains/handcuffs, suggesting imprisonment (1 mark)
• 'Mind-forg'd' = the chains are psychological, not physical — people have been conditioned to accept oppression (1 mark)
• 'Forg'd' implies something deliberately created — the ruling classes have manufactured these mental restrictions (1 mark)
• The compound adjective encapsulates Blake's belief that people must free their minds before they can free their bodies (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Agard use structure to convey his message in 'Checking Out Me History'?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of how the alternating structure (the Caribbean stanzas printed in italics against the plain type of the British stanzas) creates a visual and thematic contrast. The fragmented, short lines for heroes like Toussaint mirror spoken word poetry, asserting oral Caribbean tradition over written English convention.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments with some structural references.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Blake's use of capitalisation in 'London' (e.g. 'Church', 'Palace', 'Soldier').
practice_questions.marks:
• Capitalisation makes these nouns into proper nouns, representing specific institutions rather than general concepts (1 mark)
• 'Church' and 'Palace' are directly blamed for suffering — Blake targets the establishment (1 mark)
• 'Soldier' is capitalised to give dignity to the individual destroyed by the system (1 mark)
• The technique creates a formal, almost legal tone — as if Blake is issuing an indictment (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Agard use the image of light and nature to present Mary Seacole in 'Checking Out Me History'?
practice_questions.marks:
• 'healing star' and 'yellow sunrise' use natural imagery to elevate Seacole (1 mark)
• The light imagery contrasts with the darkness of exclusion from history (1 mark)
• 'To the dying' emphasises her compassion and bravery in conflict zones (1 mark)
• The imagery is almost divine, contrasting sharply with the mundane British figures like Dick Whittington (1 mark)

before.exam_tip_html: When comparing these poems with others in the anthology, focus on the poets’ methods rather than just their messages. Compare how Blake uses a strict ABAB rhyme scheme to create a relentless mood, while Agard uses irregular line lengths and dialect to rebel against conventional poetic form. Always link form and structure to meaning.

lessons.title: The Charge of the Light Brigade & Bayonet Charge

practice_questions.text: Compare how Tennyson in 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' and Hughes in 'Bayonet Charge' present the experience of soldiers in battle.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison. Perceptive analysis showing how Tennyson's galloping rhythm commemorates while Hughes's fractured form exposes terror. Well-integrated context.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful comparison with clear analysis of both poets' methods.
Mid band (16-20): Clear comparison with explained analysis.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comparative comments.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present attitudes to war in 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Compare language that reveals attitude (e.g. 'Honour' vs 'etcetera')
• Analyse how rhythm and form shape meaning in both poems
• Integrate context (Victorian patriotism vs post-war disillusionment)
• Use comparative connectives and precise terminology

practice_questions.text: Analyse the effect of the repetition of 'Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them, / Cannon in front of them' in Tennyson's poem.
practice_questions.marks:
• The repetition surrounds the reader as the cannons surround the soldiers (1 mark)
• Three directions creates claustrophobia — there is no escape (1 mark)
• The regular rhythm mimics the relentless firing of the cannons (1 mark)
• The listed positions emphasise the soldiers' courage in advancing despite overwhelming odds (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Hughes use the word 'etcetera' in 'Bayonet Charge' and what is its effect?
practice_questions.marks:
• 'King, honour, human dignity, etcetera' — the grand concepts are listed dismissively (1 mark)
• 'Etcetera' reduces patriotic ideals to meaningless afterthoughts (1 mark)
• In combat, abstract ideology is worthless — only survival matters (1 mark)
• The informal register of 'etcetera' within a poem is deliberately jarring (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explore how Tennyson presents the soldiers as heroic in 'The Charge of the Light Brigade'.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. The soldiers are collectively heroic ('the six hundred') rather than individually named. The imperative 'Honour the charge they made!' demands the reader's respect. 'Theirs but to do and die' presents obedience itself as heroic. Contextualises Tennyson's role as Poet Laureate.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant quotations.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the openings of 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' and 'Bayonet Charge' immediately establish the poets' different attitudes to conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Tennyson opens with rhythmic, galloping repetition ('Half a league') creating momentum and energy — war as dramatic spectacle. Hughes opens with 'Suddenly' — in medias res, disorienting, no preparation — war as chaotic terror. Both openings mirror their overall messages.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear comparison of both openings.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple observations.

before.exam_tip_html: When comparing these poems, the strongest responses will examine how the poets’ different contexts shape their attitudes. Tennyson, writing as Poet Laureate in 1854, had a duty to honour the soldiers; Hughes, writing after two world wars, could afford to be more critical. Always embed context within your analysis of language and structure — don’t treat it as a separate paragraph.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Browning in 'My Last Duchess' and one other poet present the abuse of power.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison. Perceptive analysis of how Browning uses the dramatic monologue to expose the Duke's possessiveness, compared with chosen poem's methods. Well-integrated context.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful comparison with clear analysis.
Mid band (16-20): Clear comparison with relevant quotations.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present controlling characters in 'My Last Duchess' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Analyse how the Duke's language reveals control (e.g. possessive 'my', curtain imagery)
• Compare methods of presenting control in both poems
• Discuss how historical/social context shapes power dynamics
• Explore how form (dramatic monologue) contributes to meaning

practice_questions.text: Analyse the significance of the line 'I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together.'
practice_questions.marks:
• 'Gave commands' is a euphemism that hides murder behind bureaucratic language (1 mark)
• The semicolon creates a heavy pause, mirroring the finality of death (1 mark)
• 'All smiles stopped' is devastating understatement — her joy, warmth, and life were all extinguished (1 mark)
• The Duke's casual delivery reveals his complete lack of remorse (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Browning use the Neptune sculpture to reveal the Duke's character at the end of the poem?
practice_questions.marks:
• Neptune taming a sea-horse is a metaphor for the Duke controlling others (1 mark)
• He sees himself as a god, above ordinary people (1 mark)
• The Duchess was his 'sea-horse' — beautiful but needing to be tamed (1 mark)
• Placing this at the end shows his attitudes haven't changed — he will treat his next wife the same way (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explore how Browning uses the dramatic monologue form to reveal the Duke's true character.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): The Duke believes he is presenting himself as reasonable and refined. But through careful word choices ('my', 'commands'), caesura, and euphemism, Browning reveals possessiveness, pride, and murder. The reader understands more than the Duke intends — this dramatic irony is the poem's central method.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with relevant examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: What is the effect of Browning's use of enjambment in 'My Last Duchess'?
practice_questions.marks:
• Enjambment disguises the rhyming couplets, making the poem sound like natural speech (1 mark)
• Reflects the Duke's attempt to appear casual and conversational (1 mark)
• Beneath the flowing surface, the rigid couplets represent his need for control (1 mark)
• The continuous, unbroken stanza shows the Duke monopolising the conversation (1 mark)

before.exam_tip_html: The dramatic monologue is the most important technique to analyse in this poem. Explain how the Duke reveals more than he intends — he thinks he’s justified, but the reader sees a murderer. This gap between what the speaker says and what the reader understands is called dramatic irony, and discussing it will earn you marks for analysis of the writer’s methods (AO2).

practice_questions.text: Compare how Owen in 'Exposure' and Heaney in 'Storm on the Island' present the power of nature.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison. Perceptive analysis of how both poets use nature as a destructive force — Owen literally (cold kills soldiers), Heaney metaphorically (storm as political conflict). Well-integrated context.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful comparison with clear analysis.
Mid band (16-20): Clear comparison.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present fear in 'Exposure' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Analyse specific language creating fear (e.g. 'merciless iced east winds that knive us')
• Compare how form reinforces the sense of fear (para-rhyme, half-lines)
• Integrate context (WWI trenches, The Troubles)
• Discuss the different sources and types of fear

practice_questions.text: Analyse the effect of Owen's refrain 'But nothing happens' in 'Exposure'.
practice_questions.marks:
• Creates a devastating sense of futility — the soldiers are dying from waiting, not fighting (1 mark)
• Each repetition drains more hope from the poem (1 mark)
• The anti-climax of 'nothing' undermines any expectation of heroic action (1 mark)
• Reflects Owen's message that war is not glorious but tedious, cold, and meaningless (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: What is the significance of the phrase 'huge nothing' in Heaney's 'Storm on the Island'?
practice_questions.marks:
• An oxymoron — something cannot be both 'huge' and 'nothing' (1 mark)
• Captures the paradox of fearing an invisible, intangible threat (1 mark)
• Wind/storm has no physical form but causes real destruction (1 mark)
• If read politically, suggests the fear of sectarian violence during The Troubles — terrifying but hard to define or confront (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explore how Owen uses sound and rhythm to convey the soldiers' suffering in 'Exposure'.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis. Sibilance ('merciless iced east') mimics hissing wind. Para-rhyme (wire/war) creates unresolved tension. Half-lines at stanza ends create a 'dying fall' mirroring fading strength. The refrain's flat tone reflects hopelessness.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Heaney establish and then undermine confidence in 'Storm on the Island'?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Opens with 'We are prepared' — confident, declarative. Lists practical preparations (squat houses, no hay). But as the storm arrives, confidence erodes: the sea 'spits like a tame cat turned savage', and the poem ends with fear of a 'huge nothing'. The journey from confidence to terror mirrors political complacency giving way to conflict.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple observations.

before.exam_tip_html: Both poems explore the power of nature, but the strongest exam responses will distinguish between their purposes. Owen uses nature to criticise war and the government that sends soldiers to die; Heaney uses nature as a metaphor for the political fear that preceded The Troubles. Always specify which poem you are analysing and avoid generalising about “both poets.”

practice_questions.text: Compare how Armitage in 'Remains' and Duffy in 'War Photographer' present the lasting effects of conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison. Perceptive analysis of how both poets show psychological trauma.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful comparison.
Mid band (16-20): Clear comparison.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present guilt in 'Remains' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Analyse language revealing guilt
• Compare how form reflects psychological states
• Discuss how context shapes each speaker’s guilt
• Use precise comparative language throughout

practice_questions.text: Analyse the effect of the phrase 'probably armed, possibly not' in 'Remains'.
practice_questions.marks:
• Modal verbs create moral ambiguity (1 mark)
• The soldier doesn’t know if the man was a genuine threat (1 mark)
• This uncertainty is the source of his ongoing guilt and PTSD (1 mark)
• The casual delivery makes it more disturbing (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Duffy use the contrast between England and war zones to convey her message?
practice_questions.marks:
• 'Rural England' = peaceful, comfortable, indifferent (1 mark)
• 'Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh.' = short, blunt list of real war zones (1 mark)
• The contrast criticises the gap between those who suffer and those who look away (1 mark)
• The public’s tears are shallow and quickly forgotten (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explore how Armitage uses the shift from past to present tense in 'Remains' to convey the soldier's psychological state.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Past tense tells the event as a story. Shift to present tense shows the memory replaying involuntarily. This depicts PTSD flashbacks. The tense shift mirrors loss of control.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: What is the significance of Duffy comparing the photographer to 'a priest preparing to intone a Mass'?
practice_questions.marks:
• Elevates the photographer’s work to a sacred, ritualistic act (1 mark)
• Developing photographs becomes a ceremony of remembrance (1 mark)
• Suggests he treats the dead with reverence the public does not (1 mark)
• Contrasts with newspaper readers’ casual indifference (1 mark)

before.exam_tip_html: These poems are frequently compared in the exam. To reach the top levels, analyse how both poets use form to convey psychological states: Armitage’s collapsing stanza structure reflects PTSD; Duffy’s controlled six-line stanzas reflect the photographer’s attempt to impose order on chaos. Always link your analysis of language and structure to the poets’ purposes.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Garland in 'Kamikaze' and Rumens in 'The Emigrée' present the power of memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison. In 'Kamikaze', memory of nature (fish, sun) pulls the pilot back to life; in 'The Emigrée', 'sunlight-clear' memory resists political reality. Both use light imagery but to different ends. Well-integrated context.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful comparison.
Mid band (16-20): Clear comparison.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present the impact of conflict on individuals in 'Kamikaze' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Analyse how language reveals the personal cost of conflict
• Compare structural choices (indirect speech in 'Kamikaze', light motif in chosen poem)
• Integrate cultural/historical context
• Discuss how both poets use personal perspectives to explore wider themes

practice_questions.text: Analyse the significance of the final line of 'Kamikaze': 'which had been the better way to die.'
practice_questions.marks:
• Reveals that both options (mission or return) led to 'death' — physical or social (1 mark)
• Questions whether the pilot's choice to live was worth it (1 mark)
• The word 'die' shocks — he is alive but effectively dead to his family (1 mark)
• Creates a devastating sense of irony — he survived the war but not the shame (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Rumens use light imagery to convey the speaker's relationship with her homeland?
practice_questions.marks:
• 'Sunlight-clear' makes memories glow with warmth and beauty (1 mark)
• Light imagery recurs throughout, creating resistance to negative updates (1 mark)
• The brightness represents childhood innocence and idealisation (1 mark)
• Light contrasts with the 'dark' accusation from the host society, showing a battle between memory and reality (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explore how Garland uses the pilot's silence throughout 'Kamikaze' to convey his punishment.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): The pilot never speaks directly — his story is told through indirect speech ('she said'). He is silenced within the poem just as he is silenced by his family. The daughter speaks for him because he cannot speak for himself. This structural choice mirrors the social death inflicted on him.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: What is the effect of Rumens leaving the country unnamed in 'The Emigrée'?
practice_questions.marks:
• Makes the poem universal — it could apply to any exile from any conflict (1 mark)
• Focuses on the emotional experience rather than specific politics (1 mark)
• 'There once was a country' uses fairy-tale language, making the homeland mythical (1 mark)
• Allows readers from any background to connect with the speaker's sense of loss (1 mark)

before.exam_tip_html: Both poems work well for comparison questions about identity, memory, or the impact of conflict on individuals. When analysing ‘Kamikaze’, focus on the structural silencing of the pilot (indirect speech, no direct quotation). For ‘The Emigrée’, focus on the recurring light imagery and how it resists every negative update. Always connect techniques to meaning.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Dharker in 'Tissue' and Weir in 'Poppies' use fragile objects to explore themes of power and conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison. Perceptive analysis of how paper/tissue functions differently in each poem — abstract philosophy in Dharker vs concrete domestic grief in Weir. Both end with human vulnerability.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful comparison.
Mid band (16-20): Clear comparison.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present loss in 'Poppies' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Analyse specific language conveying loss (e.g. 'playground voice catching on the wind')
• Compare structural approaches to loss
• Discuss how personal perspectives make loss tangible
• Integrate context where relevant

practice_questions.text: Analyse the significance of the final line of 'Tissue': 'turned into your skin.'
practice_questions.marks:
• Reveals the ultimate 'tissue' is human skin — the poem becomes deeply personal (1 mark)
• Skin is the most fragile structure of all, yet the most important (1 mark)
• The shift from abstract (buildings, borders) to personal (skin) is surprising and powerful (1 mark)
• Suggests human vulnerability is more valuable than any institution or construct (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: How does Weir use the poppy as a symbol in 'Poppies'?
practice_questions.marks:
• The poppy symbolises remembrance for fallen soldiers (1 mark)
• 'Spasms of paper red' links the symbol to violence as well as remembrance (1 mark)
• The mother pins it to her son's blazer — a domestic act loaded with the weight of potential loss (1 mark)
• The paper poppy is fragile — like her son, it is delicate and temporary (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explore how Dharker uses the extended metaphor of paper to challenge ideas about power.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Paper represents all human constructs: the Qur'an (faith), maps (borders), receipts (money), buildings (architecture). All are fragile. Dharker argues that if power structures were as transparent as paper, they would be less oppressive. The poem celebrates impermanence.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Weir create a sense of the mother's suppressed emotion throughout 'Poppies'?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): The mother performs domestic tasks (pinning the poppy, smoothing the blazer) as a way of controlling her emotion. 'Steeled the softening of my face' reveals what she is hiding. Sensory detail (touch, sound) makes grief physical. The final image of listening for a 'playground voice' releases the suppressed emotion in a devastating climax.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

before.exam_tip_html: When writing about ‘Tissue’, many students struggle because the poem is abstract. Focus on the extended metaphor of paper and explain what each type of paper represents (Qur’an = faith, maps = borders, receipts = money, skin = humanity). For ‘Poppies’, focus on the textile/domestic imagery and how it connects the mother’s world to the battlefield. Both poems reward close attention to individual words and images.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Wordsworth in 'The Prelude' and one other poet present the power of nature.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison. Perceptive analysis of how Wordsworth uses personification ('upreared its head') and the sublime to present nature as a transformative force, compared with the chosen poem's approach. Well-integrated Romantic context.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful comparison.
Mid band (16-20): Clear comparison.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comments.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present a shift from confidence to fear in 'The Prelude' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Track language shifts in both poems (e.g. 'lustily' to 'trembling')
• Analyse how structure mirrors psychological change
• Discuss the role of nature/conflict in creating fear
• Integrate context (Romanticism, chosen poem's context)

practice_questions.text: Analyse the effect of the personification of the mountain in 'The Prelude'.
practice_questions.marks:
• 'Upreared its head' personifies the mountain as a living creature (1 mark)
• 'Voluntary power instinct' suggests it is charged with a will of its own (1 mark)
• 'Strode after me' makes it a pursuer/predator (1 mark)
• Personification gives nature agency and power — it is not passive landscape but an active force (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: What is the significance of the boy rowing 'lustily' at the start of the extract?
practice_questions.marks:
• 'Lustily' conveys youthful energy, confidence, and pleasure (1 mark)
• Establishes the boy's belief that he is in control of nature (1 mark)
• Contrasts with 'trembling' later — this contrast structures the entire poem (1 mark)
• The confidence makes the subsequent terror more dramatic and the lesson more powerful (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Explore how Wordsworth presents the aftermath of the boy's encounter with the mountain.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): The aftermath is psychological rather than physical. 'Huge and mighty forms, that do not live like living men, moved slowly through the mind' — the images are permanent, inescapable. 'Moved slowly' suggests they will never leave. The experience has planted something in his consciousness that transforms his understanding of nature. This connects to the Romantic idea of the sublime.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Supported comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Wordsworth use the structure of the extract to convey the boy's changing relationship with nature?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Three-part structure — departure (confidence, pastoral language), the encounter (terror, personification), and aftermath (haunted, psychological). The language shifts mirror the psychological journey: 'lustily' → 'trembling' → 'grave and serious mood'. The blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) creates a conversational, reflective tone appropriate to autobiography.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple observations.

before.content_html:
William Wordsworth and Romanticism

William Wordsworth wrote The Prelude between 1798 and 1850. It is a vast autobiographical poem about the growth of the poet’s mind, and the extract studied for AQA comes from Book 1, in which the young Wordsworth steals a boat and rows across a lake at night. What begins as a confident, joyful adventure becomes a terrifying encounter with the power of nature, as a mountain appears to rise up and pursue him.

Key Fact

Wordsworth was a leading figure of the Romantic movement, which valued emotion over reason, nature over industry, and the individual over society. The Romantics believed nature had a spiritual, almost divine power that could transform human consciousness. This extract dramatises that belief through the boy’s terrifying encounter with the mountain.

The Stolen Boat Episode

The extract divides into three clear stages. First, the boy discovers a boat and rows out onto the lake in a state of youthful confidence and pleasure. Second, a mountain appears to rise up and chase him, shattering his confidence. Third, the boy returns the boat and is haunted for days by “huge and mighty forms” in his imagination. This three-part structure mirrors a moment of revelation — the boy’s understanding of his place in the world is permanently altered.

“One summer evening (led by her) I found / A little boat tied to a willow tree” — Nature (“her”) is personified as a guiding female figure, leading the boy to the boat. The calm, pastoral language (“summer evening,” “willow tree”) establishes an idyllic mood. The boy feels in harmony with nature.

“lustily / I dipped my oars into the silent lake” — The adverb “lustily” conveys youthful energy and confidence. The “silent lake” is calm and unthreatening. The boy is enjoying himself, unaware of what is about to happen. The verb “dipped” is gentle — he disturbs the water only lightly.

“a huge peak, black and huge, / As if with voluntary power instinct, / Upreared its head” — The mountain is personified as a living creature charged with “voluntary power” — it seems to choose to terrify the boy. The repetition of “huge” and the harsh consonants in “black” and “peak” create a sense of overwhelming, menacing scale. The mountain “Strode after me” — it pursues him like a predator.

“with trembling oars I turned, / And through the silent water stole my way / Back to the covert of the willow tree” — The boy’s confidence has collapsed. “Trembling” replaces “lustily.” He “stole” back — a word linking back to his original theft of the boat, but now suggesting fear and guilt rather than adventure. The “willow tree” reappears, but the return journey feels entirely different from the departure.

“huge and mighty forms, that do not live / Like living men, moved slowly through the mind” — The aftermath is psychological. The “forms” are not real — they exist in his mind — but they are described as more real than “living men.” Nature has planted something in his consciousness that will never leave. The slow rhythm of “moved slowly through the mind” suggests these images are permanent and inescapable.

Themes

The sublime: The mountain represents the Romantic concept of the sublime — something so vast and powerful that it inspires both awe and terror. The boy is humbled: he thought he was in control of nature (rowing the boat), but nature showed him he is insignificant. This encounter changes him permanently.

Nature’s moral authority: The boy stole the boat — a transgression. Nature’s response (the mountain rising) can be read as a punishment or warning. Wordsworth presents nature as having a moral dimension: it teaches, corrects, and humbles humanity. The boy returns the boat “in grave / And serious mood,” suggesting he has learned a lesson.

Key Fact

The shift from confidence to fear is reflected in the poem’s language: “lustily” becomes “trembling,” “proud” becomes “grave,” and the “silent lake” becomes a space of terror. This reversal is the poem’s central movement — from human confidence to natural dominance.

With Ozymandias: Both poems show nature overwhelming human power. In Ozymandias, the desert has erased an empire; in The Prelude, the mountain terrifies a boy. Both suggest that nature is the ultimate power, indifferent to human ambition.

With Exposure: Both present nature as hostile and overwhelming. Owen’s soldiers are killed by the cold; Wordsworth’s boy is psychologically transformed by the mountain. However, Wordsworth sees this as ultimately positive (a learning experience), while Owen sees only destruction.

With Storm on the Island: Both explore humanity’s vulnerability to nature. Heaney’s community faces a “huge nothing”; Wordsworth faces a “huge peak, black and huge.” Both poets use the word “huge” to convey nature’s overwhelming scale.

before.exam_tip_html: The extract from The Prelude is one of the best poems for comparison questions about the power of nature, conflict between humanity and nature, or the concept of the sublime. When analysing it, track the shift in language from confidence to fear (e.g. “lustily” to “trembling”). This demonstrates understanding of structure and the writer’s methods, which examiners specifically reward.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present the lasting impact of conflict in 'Remains' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (26-30) Convincing, critical comparison throughout. Perceptive analysis of both poets' methods with well-integrated context. Precise subject terminology.
Upper band (21-25) Thoughtful comparison with developed analysis.
Mid band (16-20): Clear, explained comparison.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant comparative comments.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Supported comments with limited comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present power in 'Ozymandias' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Compare how both poets present different types of power (political, natural, personal)
• Analyse language, structure, and form in both poems
• Integrate context throughout (Romantic radicalism, chosen poem's context)
• Use comparative connectives consistently

practice_questions.text: Compare how the poets present the relationship between humanity and nature in 'The Prelude' and one other poem from the anthology.
practice_questions.marks:
Strong answers will:
• Compare how both poets present nature's power over humanity
• Analyse specific techniques (personification, imagery, rhythm)
• Compare the poets' different attitudes to nature (awe vs fear vs indifference)
• Embed relevant context within analysis

practice_questions.text: Explain why choosing a poem with a contrasting attitude makes for a stronger comparison than choosing one with a similar attitude.
practice_questions.marks:
• Contrasting attitudes allow you to discuss differences as well as similarities (1 mark)
• You can compare methods (e.g. how different forms convey different attitudes) (1 mark)
• Context becomes more interesting when poets from different eras/backgrounds approach the same theme differently (1 mark)
• Examiners reward nuanced comparison — 'whereas' and 'however' show deeper thinking than 'similarly' alone (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: What is the difference between 'feature-spotting' and 'analysis', and why does it matter for your grade?
practice_questions.marks:
• Feature-spotting = naming a technique ('Shelley uses alliteration') without explaining its effect (1 mark)
• Analysis = explaining WHY the poet chose that technique and what effect it creates (1 mark)
• Feature-spotting typically sits at Level 2-3; analysis sits at Level 4-6 (1 mark)
• The examiner wants to see your interpretation of the writer's choices, not a list of techniques (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Write a PEALC paragraph comparing how Tennyson in 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' and Hughes in 'Bayonet Charge' present the experience of being a soldier.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Paragraph compares throughout using connectives. Quotations from both poems analysed for method and effect. Context integrated (Victorian patriotism vs post-war disillusionment). Precise terminology (dactylic rhythm, in medias res).
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear comparison with relevant quotations.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some comparison attempted.
Lower band (1-2): Describes rather than compares.

glossary_terms.definition: The total marks for the poetry comparison question in AQA English Literature Paper 2 Section B, assessed across AO1 (response to text), AO2 (analysis of methods), and AO3 (context).
A planning technique for poetry comparison: identify 3 points of comparison, each with a quotation from both poems, and note the method and context for each.

A structure for comparative paragraphs: Point (comparative statement), Evidence (quotation from poem A), Analysis (method + effect), Link (quotation from poem B with comparison), Context (relevant background for both poems).

before.exam_tip_html: Aim for three comparative paragraphs in 45 minutes (5 minutes planning, 35 minutes writing, 5 minutes checking). Each paragraph should discuss both poems together. The strongest responses will compare not just what the poems say (AO1) but how they say it (AO2 — language, structure, form) and why (AO3 — context). Remember: you choose the second poem, so pick one you know well and can analyse in detail.
